A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PRIMT research. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching material moved around the relocated checklist.

before.justification: v1 reports original robotics experiments, component ablations, preference-label and reward-alignment analyses, and Kinova robot demonstrations in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds bimanual manipulation results, a dense-reward comparison, numerical reward-alignment scores, physical-robot success counts and resource analyses.

M1.justification: The keyframe extraction, hierarchical preference fusion, foresight generation, hindsight augmentation and causal auxiliary loss remain unchanged. Newly described deployment safeguards document implementation details without establishing a revision to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Appendix G.6 adds RoboSuite TwoArmPegInHole, extending evaluation to coordinated bimanual manipulation. The original eight simulation tasks and two physical-robot tasks remain. The human-cost estimates do not represent an added human study.

E2.justification: Appendix G.7 introduces GT, SAC trained directly with ground-truth dense rewards, alongside the existing methods in Figure 23. This differs from the retained scripted-preference oracle PrefGT. The original baseline and ablation memberships remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The added evaluations introduce dense-reward SAC training, maximum/mean/final success summaries for the bimanual task, R2 reward-alignment scoring and resource-efficiency metrics. The original simulation settings and hyperparameter tables are retained.

E4.justification: Appendix G.8 adds numerical R2 analysis of reward alignment for PRIMT, its hindsight and causal-loss ablations, and RL-VLM-F across seven tasks. Section 4.5 and Appendix H.1 add cost-performance analyses. The existing component ablations, backbone study and trajectory case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Appendix G.9 first reports 10 randomized physical-robot trials per model; v1 supplied no trial count. This is newly disclosed repetition information, not evidence of increased runs. The five-seed simulation reporting remains unchanged, and no new confidence intervals or significance tests are supplied.

E6.justification: The original learning curves are retained, but substantial result blocks are added: dense-reward GT curves, seven-task R2 scores, resource tables and bimanual results. Table 4 reports final success of 64.15% for PRIMT, 32.66% for RL-VLM-F and 78.03% for PrefGT. Appendix G.9 newly reports lifting/stacking successes of 7/10 and 6/10 for PRIMT versus 4/10 and 2/10 for PrefCLM.

T1.justification: Table 7 introduces an explicit efficiency definition: average performance gain divided by average resource increase. The existing mathematical formulation, PSL derivations and assumptions remain unchanged, with no added theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and introductory contributions retain the same scientific claims. The conclusion adds a claim that PRIMT balances performance and cost-effectiveness to support scalable preference learning, and describes its human-effort benefit as reduction.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations concerning potential bimanual generalization, proximity to dense-reward performance and the justification of additional model costs. Appendix H.1 replaces the qualitative cost caveat with quantified trade-off arguments and removes the specific warning that transfer beyond robotics may require adapting prompts, objectives or modality alignment; such transfer remains future work in the conclusion.

D1.justification: The physical-robot section newly describes dynamics randomization, sensor modelling, simulation-to-hardware configuration matching and rejection of actions exceeding motion thresholds. Appendix H.1 adds training times and the assumptions behind API and human-annotation cost estimates. These expand documentation; the core implementation settings and code-access statements remain unchanged.

R1.justification: The 64 references and related-work discussion are unchanged. The positioning relative to earlier foundation-model feedback and preference-learning methods remains the same.

P1.justification: v2 converts baseline and ablation descriptions into bullets, separates additional experiments from real-world deployment, expands the conclusion and adds acknowledgments. It moves the checklist before the appendices and updates the contents listing, while retaining most scientific prose.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 4–7 and the dense-reward comparison in Figure 23, enlarges Figures 3 and 5, and adjusts supplementary figure placement. Existing plots and demonstrations are retained; the former real-world Figure 23 becomes Figure 24.

improvement.justification: v2 makes previously visual reward-alignment and robot-performance evidence more assessable through Table 5 and explicit success counts, while adding a useful dense-reward reference and deployment details. These are concrete gains, but new evaluation and uncertainty documentation remains limited. The cost argument also has incomplete Table 7 entries and substitutes scripted PrefGT performance for measured human feedback, limiting the strength of the new efficiency claims.
